source_text: Καὶ ἕσπερος ἀστέρων κάλλιστος, οὐ διὰ τὸ ἀναλογοῦντα ἔχειν τὰ μέρη ἐξ ὧν συνέστηκεν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ ἄλυπόν τινα καὶ ἡδεῖαν τὴν ἀπ' αὐτοῦ αὐγὴν ἐμπίπτειν τοῖς ὄμμασιν. Ἔπειτα νῦν ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ κρίσις περὶ τοῦ καλοῦ, οὐ πάντως πρὸς τὸ ἐν ὄψει τερπνὸν ἀποβλέποντος, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τὴν εἰς ὕστερον ἀπ' αὐτοῦ ὠφέλειαν προορωμένου γεγένηται. Ὀφθαλμοὶ γὰρ οὔπω ἦσαν κριτικοὶ τοῦ ἐν φωτὶ κάλλους. Καὶ διεχώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ φωτὸς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ σκότους. Τουτέστιν, ἄμικτον αὐτῶν τὴν φύσιν καὶ κατ' ἐναντίωσιν ἀντικειμένην ὁ Θεὸς κατεσκεύασε. Πλείστῳ γὰρ τῷ μέσῳ διέστηκεν ἀπ' ἀλλήλων αὐτὰ καὶ διώρισεν. 2.8 Καὶ ἐκάλεσεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ φῶς ἡμέραν, καὶ τὸ σκότος ἐκάλεσε νύκτα. Νῦν μὲν λοιπὸν μετὰ τὴν ἡλίου γένεσιν ἡμέρα ἐστὶν, ὁ ὑπὸ ἡλίου πεφωτισμένος ἀὴρ, ἐν τῷ ὑπὲρ γῆν ἡμισφαιρίῳ λάμποντος, καὶ νὺξ σκίασμα γῆς ἀποκρυπτομένου ἡλίου γινόμενον. Τότε δὲ οὐ κατὰ κίνησιν ἡλιακὴν, ἀλλ' ἀναχεομένου τοῦ πρωτογόνου φωτὸς ἐκείνου, καὶ πάλιν συστελλομένου κατὰ τὸ ὁρισθὲν μέτρον παρὰ Θεοῦ, ἡμέρα ἐγένετο, καὶ νὺξ ἀντεπῄει. Καὶ ἐγένετο ἑσπέρα, καὶ ἐγένετο πρωῒ, ἡμέρα μία. Ἑσπέρα μὲν οὖν ἐστι κοινὸς ὅρος ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός· καὶ πρωΐα ὁμοίως ἡ γειτονία νυκτὸς πρὸς ἡμέραν. Ἵνα τοίνυν τὰ πρεσβεῖα τῆς γενέσεως ἀποδῷ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, πρότερον εἶπε τὸ πέρας τῆς ἡμέρας, εἶτα τὸ τῆς νυκτὸς, ὡς ἐφεπομένης τῆς νυκτὸς τῇ ἡμέρᾳ. Ἡ γὰρ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως τοῦ φωτὸς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ κατάστασις, οὐχὶ νὺξ ἦν, ἀλλὰ σκότος· τὸ μέντοι ἀντιδιασταλὲν πρὸς τὴν ἡμέραν, τοῦτο νὺξ ὠνομάσθη· ὅπερ νεωτέρας καὶ τῆς προσηγορίας μετὰ τὴν ἡμέραν τετύχηκεν. Ἐγένετο οὖν ἑσπέρα, καὶ ἐγένετο πρωΐ. Τὸ ἡμερονύκτιον λέγει. Καὶ οὐκέτι προσηγόρευσεν, ἡμέρα καὶ νὺξ, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐπικρα τοῦντι τὴν πᾶσαν προσηγορίαν ἀπένειμε. Ταύτην ἂν καὶ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ Γραφῇ τὴν συνήθειαν εὕροις, ἐν τῇ τοῦ χρόνου μετρήσει ἡμέρας ἀριθμουμένας, οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ νύκτας μετὰ τῶν ἡμερῶν. Αἱ ἡμέραι τῶν ἐτῶν ἡμῶν, ὁ ψαλμῳδός φησιν. Καὶ πάλιν ὁ Ἰακώβ· Αἱ ἡμέραι τῆς ζωῆς μου μικραὶ καὶ πονηραί. Καὶ πάλιν, Πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς μου. Ὥστε τὰ νῦν ἐν ἱστορίας εἴδει παραδοθέντα νομοθεσία ἐστὶ πρὸς τὰ ἑξῆς. Καὶ ἐγένετο ἑσπέρα, καὶ ἐγένετο πρωῒ, ἡμέρα μία. Τίνος ἕνεκεν οὐκ εἶπε πρώτην, ἀλλὰ μίαν; καίτοιγε ἀκολουθότερον ἦν τὸν μέλλοντα ἐπάγειν δευτέραν καὶ τρίτην καὶ τετάρτην ἡμέραν, τὴν κατάρχουσαν τῶν ἐφεξῆς πρώτην προσαγορεῦσαι. Ἀλλὰ μίαν εἶπεν, ἤτοι τὸ μέτρον ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς περιορίζων, καὶ συνάπτων τοῦ ἡμερονυκτίου τὸν χρόνον, ὡς τῶν εἰκοσιτεσσάρων ὡρῶν μιᾶς ἡμέρας ἐκπληρουσῶν διάστημα, συνυπακουομένης δηλονότι τῇ ἡμέρᾳ καὶ τῆς νυκτὸς, ὥστε κἂν ἐν ταῖς τροπαῖς τοῦ ἡλίου συμβαίνῃ τὴν ἑτέραν αὐτῶν ὑπερβάλλειν, ἀλλὰ τῷ γε ἀφωρισμένῳ χρόνῳ ἐμπεριγράφεσθαι πάντως ἀμφοτέρων τὰ διαστήματα· ὡς ἂν εἰ ἔλεγε, τὸ τῶν τεσσάρων καὶ εἴκοσιν ὡρῶν μέτρον, μιᾶς ἐστιν ἡμέρας διάστημα· ἢ, ἡ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ σημείου ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ πάλιν ἀποκατάστασις ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ γίνεται· ὥστε ὁσάκις ἂν ἑσπέρα καὶ πρωΐα κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ἡλίου περιφορὰν ἐπιλαμβάνῃ τὸν κόσμον, μὴ ἐν πλείονι χρόνῳ, ἀλλ' ἐν μιᾶς ἡμέρας διαστήματι τὴν περίοδον ἐκπληροῦσθαι.
thought_title: Why the first day is called one, not first
orientation: Basil is explaining Genesis 1:5, arguing that God's judgment that light was good looked to future benefit, and that the first day is called 'one' to define the measure of a day-night cycle.
pass_a_gloss: And the evening star is most beautiful of stars, not because it has proportionate parts from which it is composed, but because a painless and pleasant radiance from it falls upon the eyes. Then now the judgment of God about the beautiful has come to be, not at all looking toward what is delightful in sight, but also foreseeing the benefit from it for later. For eyes were not yet judges of the beauty in light. And God separated between the light and between the darkness. That is, God made their nature unmixed and opposed in contrariety. For by the greatest interval he separated them from one another and divided them. And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night. Now then henceforth after the sun's creation day is the air illuminated by the sun, shining in the hemisphere above the earth, and night is the shadow of the earth, occurring when the sun is hidden. But then not according to solar movement, but when that firstborn light was poured forth and again contracted according to the measure defined by God, day came to be, and night came in turn. And evening came to be, and morning came to be, one day. Evening then is the common boundary of day and night; and morning likewise is the neighborhood of night toward day. In order then to give the privileges of birth to the day, he first said the end of the day, then that of the night, as the night following after the day. For the state in the world before the creation of the light was not night, but darkness; what was however set in opposition to the day, this was named night; which indeed obtained both a newer name and the appellation after the day. Evening came to be then, and morning came to be. He means the day-night. And no longer did he name it day and night, but he assigned the whole appellation to the prevailing one. You would find this custom also in all the Scripture, in the measuring of time days being counted, but not also nights with the days. The days of our years, the psalmist says. And again Jacob: The days of my life are small and evil. And again, All the days of my life. So that the things now handed down in the form of history are legislation for what follows. And evening came to be, and morning came to be, one day. For what reason did he not say first, but one? And yet it would have been more consistent for the one about to bring in a second and third and fourth day to call the one beginning the subsequent ones first. But he said one, either defining the measure of day and night, and joining together the time of the day-night, as the interval of twenty-four hours completing one day, the night being understood together with the day, so that even if in the turnings of the sun it happens that one of them exceeds, yet by the appointed time the intervals of both are altogether circumscribed; as if he were saying, the measure of twenty-four hours is the interval of one day; or, the return of the heaven from the same point to the same point again happens in one day; so that as often as evening and morning according to the sun's circuit overtake the world, the period is completed not in more time, but in the interval of one day.

choices.term: ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ φωτὸς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ σκότους
choices.english: between the light and between the darkness
choices.why: Preserves the doubled Hebrew idiom of the Septuagint, which Basil quotes exactly; flattening it would lose the scriptural texture.
rejected: between the light and the darkness

choices.why: Basil uses 'firstborn' to mark the light of day one as prior to the sun, not merely 'original' or 'primordial'; the term carries temporal priority.
Basil coins or uses a compound for the full 24-hour cycle; a hyphenated compound renders it literally and keeps the coinage visible.
πρεσβεῖα means rights of the firstborn or precedence; 'privileges of birth' keeps the honorific, birth-order sense Basil is arguing for.
Basil contrasts the narrative form with its legislative force; 'form of history' keeps the genre term without importing 'story' or 'account'.
rejected: in the manner of a narrative

choices.why: τροπαί are the solstices or seasonal turnings; 'turnings' is literal and avoids the technical 'solstices' which would narrow Basil's point about varying day and night lengths.

pass_b_english: And the evening star is the most beautiful of the stars, not because its parts are in proportion to one another, but because its radiance falls on the eyes in a way that is painless and pleasant. Then again, God's judgment about the beautiful was made not only with a view to what delights the sight, but also with foresight of the benefit that would come from it later. For there were as yet no eyes to judge the beauty in light. And God separated between the light and between the darkness (Genesis 1:4). That is, God made their natures unmixed and opposed to one another in contrariety. For he set them apart and divided them by the greatest distance.

And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night (Genesis 1:5). Now, after the creation of the sun, day is the air lit by the sun when it shines in the hemisphere above the earth, and night is the shadow of the earth that occurs when the sun is hidden. But then it was not according to the sun's movement; rather, as that firstborn light was poured forth and again contracted according to the measure fixed by God, day came to be, and night followed in turn. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day (Genesis 1:5). Evening, then, is the common boundary of day and night; and morning likewise is the neighborhood of night to day. So in order to give the privileges of birth to the day, he first named the end of the day, and then the end of the night, since night follows after day. For the state of the world before the creation of light was not night, but darkness; what was set in contrast to the day was named night, and it received this newer name after the day. So there was evening, and there was morning. He means the day-night. And he no longer named them day and night, but assigned the whole name to the prevailing one. You would find this same custom throughout all Scripture: in the measuring of time, days are counted, and not nights along with the days. The days of our years, says the psalmist (Psalm 89:10 LXX, Hebrew 90:10). And again Jacob: The days of my life are few and evil (Genesis 47:9). And again: All the days of my life (Psalm 26:4 LXX, Hebrew 27:4). So what has now been handed down in the form of history is legislation for what follows. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day (Genesis 1:5). Why did he not say first, but one? And yet it would have been more consistent for the one who was about to bring in a second, third, and fourth day to call the day that begins the sequence first. But he said one, either defining the boundary of the measure of day and night and joining together the time of the day-night, since the twenty-four hours complete the interval of one day—night being clearly included along with the day—so that even if at the turnings of the sun one of them happens to exceed the other, the intervals of both are nevertheless always circumscribed within the appointed time. It is as if he were saying: the measure of twenty-four hours is the interval of one day; or, the return of the heaven from the same point to the same point again happens in one day. So however often evening and morning overtake the world according to the sun's circuit, the period is completed not in more time, but in the interval of one day.
